question: Which germ is the main cause of Tuberculosis (TB)?
explanation: You've got this! TB is caused by a tough germ called Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Knowing your causative agents is key on the wards!

question: Why do TB patients have to take a combination of multiple drugs instead of just one?

options.A: To prevent the patient from experiencing any side effects
options.B: To shorten the entire treatment course to one week
options.C: To prevent the development of drug-resistant bacterial strains
options.D: To make the medication taste better for the patient

explanation: Using a mix of drugs stops the sneaky TB germs from mutating and becoming resistant to treatment. Great nursing insight!

question: Which common anti-TB drug is famous for turning urine and tears a harmless red-orange color?
explanation: Rifampicin gives body fluids a reddish tint. As a nurse, warning your patients about this beforehand saves them a lot of panic!

question: What is the main job of Ethambutol when given with other TB medications?

options.A: Destroying the liver enzymes that break down other drugs
options.B: Killing all dormant bacteria within the first week
options.C: Preventing the emergence of bacterial resistance
options.D: Relieving joint pains caused by pyrazinamide

explanation: Ethambutol acts as a solid backup team member, stopping the bacteria from building resistance while the other drugs do the heavy lifting.

question: How does Rifampicin stop TB bacteria from multiplying?

options.A: By dissolving the patient's lung tissue
options.C: By destroying the human liver cells

explanation: Rifampicin targets bacterial RNA synthesis, halting the germ's ability to make essential proteins and grow.

question: Why do regular antibiotics like standard penicillin fail against tuberculosis?

options.A: Penicillin only works on viruses, and TB is a fungus
options.B: Human stomach acid destroys penicillin before it reaches the lungs
options.C: The waxy outer cell wall of TB blocks standard drugs from entering
options.D: Tuberculosis bacteria move too fast for penicillin to catch them

explanation: TB bacteria have a tough, waxy outer coat that standard antibiotics just can't break through. That's why special anti-TB drugs are a must!

question: What is the main goal of the intensive phase of TB treatment?

options.A: To test if the patient is allergic to all four drugs
options.B: To rapidly reduce the bacterial load and stop infectiousness
options.C: To rebuild the damaged lung tissue back to normal
options.D: To completely finish the entire course of treatment

explanation: Hitting TB hard with four drugs quickly drops the germ count so the patient stops spreading it to others. Excellent clinical milestone!

question: What actually happens during DOTS (Directly Observed Therapy) for a TB patient?

options.A: A health worker watches the patient swallow every dose
options.B: Blood tests are run daily to measure drug levels in the serum
options.C: The patient reports their pill intake via phone once a week
options.D: Family members check the pill bottles at the end of each month

explanation: Under DOTS, a healthcare worker physically watches the patient take their meds to ensure they finish the whole course without missing days.

question: Which anti-TB drug is known to cause vision issues like optic neuritis?
explanation: Ethambutol can mess with the optic nerve. That's why checking a patient's eyesight and color vision during treatment is a key nursing duty!

question: A patient taking Isoniazid complains of numbness and tingling in their feet. What vitamin supplement should you expect the doctor to prescribe?
explanation: Isoniazid can drain Vitamin B6 levels, causing nerve tingling. Giving Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) prevents and fixes this uncomfortable side effect.

question: Multi-Drug Resistant TB (MDR-TB) means the bacteria are resistant to which two key drugs?
explanation: MDR-TB specifically means the two heavy-hitters of first-line treatment—isoniazid and rifampicin—no longer work against the strain.

question: Why is drug-resistant TB so much harder to treat than regular TB?

options.A: Second-line drugs are more toxic, expensive, and require longer treatment courses
options.B: Patients with resistant TB no longer need to take medications every day
options.C: Resistant bacteria do not cause any symptoms, making patients ignore treatment
options.D: Second-line drugs only work when injected directly into the lung tissue

explanation: Backup drugs come with heavier side effects, cost more, and take much longer to work, making patient support super important.

question: A patient says, 'My cough is gone after a month, so I want to stop my TB pills.' What is your best response as a nurse?

options.A: Take only the rifampicin and throw away the other pills since they cause too many side effects
options.B: Stop the drugs immediately since the absence of a cough proves the lungs are fully healed
options.C: Switch to half the dose for the remaining months to save money on prescription refills
options.D: Continue taking all pills for the full months prescribed to kill hidden germs and prevent resistance

explanation: Feeling better doesn't mean the germs are gone! Patients must finish their full course to wipe out hidden bacteria and avoid resistance.

question: If a patient is taking Ethambutol, what regular assessment should you prioritize?

options.A: Visual acuity and color discrimination testing
options.B: Palpation of peripheral pulses in the upper extremities
options.C: Auscultation of bowel sounds and abdominal girth measurement
options.D: Daily checking of deep tendon reflexes in the legs

explanation: Keep an eye on their eyes! Regular vision and color checks catch Ethambutol's eye-related side effects early before they cause permanent harm.
